A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same dataset-generation framework, renamed from UNIGEN to DATAGEN. Their complete main texts, appendices, equations, tables, and rendered figures support reliable comparison, including matching relocated content.

before.justification: v3 reports original dataset-generation experiments, module evaluations, human assessments, benchmarking results, and data-augmentation outcomes, including Tables 2–7 and Figure 8.

after.justification: v4 retains those empirical results and adds an Alpaca/MT-Bench experiment in Table 8 and additional diversity measurements in Table 14.

M1.justification: The generation procedure retains the same example selection, attribute guidance, self-reflection, code verification, RAG validation, difficulty enhancement, and duplicate filtering. The prompt templates are unchanged. Renaming the framework and adding a code skeleton do not establish an algorithmic change.

E1.justification: v4 adds general instruction tuning using Alpaca and evaluation on MT-Bench, extending coverage to instruction-following responses across two turns. The existing benchmarking datasets, task-specific augmentation studies, and language-constraint scenarios remain.

E2.justification: The new MT-Bench experiment compares synthetic-data fine-tuning against an untuned base model and fine-tuning on original Alpaca data. Existing experimental comparator sets are unchanged. The additional frameworks in Table 1 are literature comparisons, not newly evaluated experimental baselines.

E3.justification: The new instruction-tuning experiment uses 1,000 generated examples versus 1,000 original Alpaca examples and reports first-turn, second-turn, and average MT-Bench scores. Appendix F adds APS and INGF diversity metrics. Existing generation sizes, inference settings, and task-specific fine-tuning protocols remain unchanged.

E4.justification: v4 adds an original-versus-generated diversity analysis using APS and INGF on four datasets in Table 14. Existing module evaluations, temperature sensitivity, embedding analysis, human evaluations, error analysis, and cost analysis are retained. Moving temperature and embedding analyses into the main text does not constitute new analysis.

E5.justification: Both versions retain the same averaging across five human evaluators and the same distribution plots. v4 adds no repeated-run counts, seeds, confidence intervals, significance tests, or other uncertainty-reporting procedures.

E6.justification: New Table 8 reports MT-Bench averages of 6.403 for generated-data fine-tuning, 5.259 for original-data fine-tuning, and 2.038 for the base model. New Table 14 reports worse generated-data APS on all four datasets and worse INGF on three, under the stated metric directions. Matched existing tables and plotted results are unchanged.

T1.justification: The dataset-generation expression, attribute-conditioned generation notation, Euclidean-distance filtering rule, and supervised fine-tuning loss are retained. Neither version adds or revises theoretical assumptions, propositions, proofs, or derivations; the additional diversity metrics receive only descriptive explanations.

C1.justification: The central claims remain a unified, controllable textual dataset-generation framework that supports diversity, truthfulness, dynamic benchmarking, and data augmentation. The abstract and conclusion preserve this scope. The instruction-tuning experiment supplies additional support for the existing generality claim.

C2.justification: Section 3.8 newly interprets the Alpaca comparison as evidence that DATAGEN produces useful, high-quality, diverse instruction-tuning data. Existing explanations and limitations concerning factual errors, knowledge-intensive tasks, application specificity, and alignment remain. The new APS/INGF findings are not reconciled with the retained diversity interpretation.

D1.justification: New Appendix K exposes a class interface and defaults, including five few-shot examples, a 1,000-token limit, and two workers, but leaves function implementations as placeholders. Section 3.1 newly states that generation models share prompt templates. These are documentation additions; the previously reported experimental hyperparameters and hardware remain unchanged.

R1.justification: Table 1 adds five related frameworks, including MetaMath, Qameleon, and the work introducing Prompt2Model. References also add works such as GSM-Symbolic, Magpie, and AutoBench-V, while dropping SafetyBench, HallusionBench, and the cited ChatGPT red-teaming study. The overall positioning as a unified generation framework remains.

P1.justification: v4 renames the framework and title, updates author information, shortens contribution summaries, and removes the brief four-module overview. Related work moves from main Section 2 to Appendix B, while temperature and embedding discussions move into Section 3.2. Most explanatory prose remains substantially intact.

P2.justification: v4 adds Tables 8 and 14, expands Table 1, enlarges and relocates existing displays, and adopts conference formatting and revised prompt typography. The embedding figure moves into the main text. The augmentation chart retains its values but loses explicit model row labels; annotation screenshots lose their UNIGEN title.

improvement.justification: The size-matched Alpaca comparison in Table 8 provides a more informative control for synthetic-data usefulness than v3's vanilla-versus-fine-tuned comparisons. Additional diversity measurements and interface documentation modestly improve evaluation breadth and transparency. The gains are limited: Appendix K remains a skeleton, uncertainty reporting is unchanged, and Table 14's mostly unfavorable diversity comparisons are not reconciled with existing claims.
